title: After This, So Because of This?
objective: After this level you can spot the post hoc fallacy, which treats "came first" as "caused it".
summary: Post hoc, ergo propter hoc: 'after this, therefore because of this'. Coming first is a clue, never proof, as the rooster and the lucky seat show.

cards.headline: Every morning the rooster crows. Then the sun comes up. Case closed?
cards.body: The order is perfect, day after day. Yet nobody thinks a bird hauls the sun over the horizon. So what exactly is wrong with the rooster's reasoning? And where do the rest of us make the very same move?

cards.headline: After this, therefore because of this
cards.body: Notice that B follows A, then hastily conclude that A caused B, and you've committed the post hoc fallacy. Its full Latin name is post hoc, ergo propter hoc: "after this, therefore because of this." It's one of the false cause fallacies. The rooster is the textbook case, because the only evidence offered is that the sunrise came after the crowing.

cards.headline: Why it's so tempting
cards.body: It feels right because causes really do come first: an effect never comes before its cause. And a pattern can be a genuine clue. Correlations are often good evidence of a causal link. So the mistake isn't noticing the order. It's the hasty jump from "came first" to "caused it" without checking anything else.

cards.headline: The lucky seat
cards.body: A basketball fan notices that every time he buys a good seat, his team wins, and every time he buys a cheap one, they lose. So the good seat must be causing the wins. It's an accidental pattern that tells him nothing about why the team wins, and it probably won't hold up. Still, a good seat is a good seat.

cards.headline: Post hoc: spotted
learned: Post hoc: "after this, therefore because of this"
Coming first is a clue, never proof
Causes do come before their effects
The lucky seat is an accidental pattern

questions.prompt: Match each part of the post hoc lesson with its description.

pairs.right: After this, therefore because of this

questions.explanation: Post hoc, ergo propter hoc means "after this, therefore because of this". The rooster is the textbook case, and the fan's lucky seat is an accidental pattern.

questions.prompt: Why is "the rooster crows, then the sun rises" weak evidence that crowing causes sunrise?

options.label: Roosters crow at many other times too
options.rationale: Maybe, but the real flaw is relying on order alone.

options.label: The sun rises at different times each day
options.rationale: Sunrise times vary, but that isn't the flaw.

options.label: Coming first is the only evidence offered
Nobody has timed the rooster carefully
options.rationale: Better timing would still show only order.

questions.explanation: Order alone can't show cause. Without any other check, it's just after this, therefore because of this.

questions.prompt: How does Level 41's rewind test settle the rooster question?

options.label: Replay it without the crowing: the sun still rises
Replay it with two roosters: the sun rises twice
options.rationale: Adding a rooster doesn't test what happens without one.

options.label: Replay it at night: the rooster stays quiet
options.rationale: That changes the time, not whether crowing matters.

options.label: Replay it with a hen: nobody crows at all
options.rationale: The test removes the crowing and asks about the sunrise.

questions.explanation: Take the supposed cause away. If the effect still happens, it wasn't the cause.
